section.title: Hearing and Doing the Word
section.sectionRationale: Having said God gives new birth through the word of truth, James now asks what that implanted word should produce. It is not enough to hear it; the word must be received humbly and then obeyed. He confronts the self-deception of the hearer who forgets, holds up the mirror of the perfect law of liberty, and defines the religion God actually accepts.
section.thesis: The word that saves must be humbly received and actively obeyed; merely hearing it deceives us, but the one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and does it, bridling his tongue and caring for the helpless, practices religion pure before God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: quick to hear and slow to speak; doers and not hearers only; and the marks of religion pure and undefiled.

units.label: Quick to hear, slow to speak

verses.text: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to {{orge|anger}},
for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the {{logos|word}} planted in you, which can save your souls.
Be {{poietes|doers}} of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves.
For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror,
and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like.
But the one who looks intently into the {{nomoseleutherias|perfect law of freedom}}, and continues to do so, not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer, he will be blessed in what he does.

units.label: Religion pure and undefiled
units.note: bridle the tongue, care for the helpless

verses.text: If anyone considers himself {{threskeia|religious}} and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless.
Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

orge.gloss: Settled anger or wrath, more than a passing flash of temper. James says human anger does not produce the righteousness God desires, so believers are to be slow to it. Uncontrolled anger closes the ear to the word and works against the life God is forming.

logos.gloss: Word, the message of truth by which God gives new birth, verse 18. Here it is the implanted word, planted in the heart, that has power to save. It must be received with humility and then obeyed, not merely heard.

poietes.gloss: A doer, one who makes or performs; the word can also mean a poet, one who brings something into being. James wants doers of the word, not hearers only. Genuine faith is not passive reception but active obedience that puts the word into practice.

nomoseleutherias.gloss: The law of liberty, the perfect law of freedom. Far from enslaving, God's word in Christ frees us to become what we were made to be. To gaze into it and keep gazing, then to do it, is the path of blessing, unlike the mirror-glancer who forgets.

threskeia.gloss: Religion in the sense of outward worship and religious practice, ceremony and observance. James does not despise it but redefines it: the religion God accepts bridles the tongue, cares for orphans and widows, and stays unstained by the world. Ritual without such fruit he calls worthless.

basic.context: James keeps pressing the point that real faith shows up in life. Be quick to listen and slow to speak and slow to get angry, he says, because angry words never produce the righteous life God wants. Receive the word humbly, like a seed planted in you, and then, crucially, do it. Just hearing the Bible and not obeying it is like glancing in a mirror and instantly forgetting your own face. The one who looks hard into God's freeing word and keeps doing it is blessed. Then James gives concrete tests of true religion: a controlled tongue, care for the vulnerable, and a life kept clean from the world.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is heavily prescriptive; James is issuing commands for how the new-born believer must live. The main interpretive care is to see that James is not opposing faith to works but insisting that saving faith works. The word that saves in verse 21 is the same word that must be done in verse 22. Hearing without doing is not a lesser Christianity; James calls it self-deception.
basic.originalLanguages: The word is logos, the implanted, saving message that must be received and obeyed. James wants poietes, doers, not merely hearers. The standard is the nomos tes eleutherias, the perfect law of liberty, God's freeing word. And true threskeia, religion, is measured not by ceremony but by a bridled tongue, mercy to the helpless, and an unstained life.
basic.typology: The implanted word recalls the new covenant promise of God's law written on the heart. The perfect law of liberty fulfills the Old Testament law, now internalized and freeing in Christ. Care for orphans and widows carries forward God's ancient concern for the defenseless, fulfilled in the compassion of Jesus.
basic.christ: The perfect law of liberty is God's word centered in Christ, who said the truth would set us free. Jesus is the great doer of the word, who did the Father's will perfectly. And His care for the outcast and helpless is the pattern for the pure religion James describes, mercy to orphans, widows, and the distressed.
basic.god: God gives the saving word and desires a righteousness that mere human anger can never produce. He is called our God and Father, and the religion He accepts reflects His own heart: care for the fatherless and the widow, whose defender He has always been. He looks past ceremony to the life it does or does not produce.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with the same test: hearing His words and doing them, Matthew 7:24-27. Paul says the doers of the law will be justified, Romans 2:13. God defends the orphan and widow in Deuteronomy 10:18 and Psalm 68:5. And Proverbs repeatedly links wisdom to controlled speech.
basic.oneStory: God has always wanted a people who not only hear His word but live it, from Israel commanded to do and not merely listen, to the new covenant word written on the heart. James applies this to the scattered church: the word that gave them new birth must now bear fruit in obedient, merciful lives. This is the shape of the freedom Christ brings, and it points to the day when God's people fully do His will.

context.literary:
The passage is built as a small ring that begins and ends on speech. Verse 19 opens with the ear and the mouth, quick to listen, slow to speak, and verse 26 closes the unit with the bridled tongue, so that the whole section sits between two warnings about words. Inside the ring James moves in three beats. Verses 19 to 21 are commands, a short run of imperatives about the ear, the temper and the heart. Verses 22 to 25 are the picture, one extended image of a man at a mirror set against a man who stoops over the law. Verses 26 and 27 are the proof, two tests that read like a definition but are really examples of how the word, once received, looks in daily life.

The hinge is verse 22, where James turns from receiving to doing and names the danger, self deception. Notice how he reasons backward from the mirror. He does not say the hearer forgets the word; he says the hearer forgets his own face. The word is treated as something that tells the truth about the listener, which is why a quick glance and a walk away is so foolish. The contrast between the two men is also a contrast of verbs: the first one looks, goes away and forgets, three quick actions in a row, while the second looks intently, continues, and becomes a doer. The quiet detail is the second man's staying power. James describes him with a participle of remaining, which makes obedience a long habit rather than a single decision.

The unit also looks back to verse 18, where God gave us birth by the word of truth, and forward to chapter 2. The two tests of verse 27, care for the weak and separation from the world, are exactly the themes the next chapters take up, favoritism toward the rich in chapter 2 and friendship with the world in chapter 4.
context.historical:
James writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad, James 1:1, and he assumes that their gatherings revolved around the reading of Scripture. In the synagogue tradition hearing was the centre of worship, as the Shema begins with the command to hear, Deuteronomy 6:4. A community that prized hearing could slide into counting attendance as obedience, and that is the danger James names. Greek and Jewish moral teachers alike warned against talk that outran life, so his image of the glance in a mirror would have been immediately understood.

Mirrors in the first century were not the glass we know. They were commonly polished bronze or other metal, which gave a real but imperfect reflection. The picture therefore fits well: a person sees a face and sees it dimly, and a quick look leaves little in the memory. James's point does not depend on the quality of the mirror, but the ordinary experience of a hurried glance fits his argument.

The closing verses speak into a world with almost no safety net for the poor. Orphans and widows had no legal standing to claim an inheritance or to bring a case, and their survival depended on the generosity of relatives and the community. The law of Moses had made them a standing charge on Israel, Deuteronomy 10:18 and 24:19 to 21, and the prophets rebuked the nation for neglecting them, Isaiah 1:17. When James calls care for them the shape of pure religion before God, he is using a measure his readers already knew from their Scriptures. The word he uses for religion points to outward expression, the visible practice of worship, so the claim is that the most visible form of worship God looks for is mercy in action.
context.canonical:
The theme that hearing must become doing is one of the oldest in Scripture. At Sinai the people answered God with 'We will do everything the LORD has said,' Exodus 24:7, and the psalmist's blessing is on the one whose delight is in the law of the LORD, Psalm 1:1 to 2. The prophets complained that Israel heard and did not do, Ezekiel 33:31, and Moses had warned that the word was near them, in their mouth and heart, so that they might do it, Deuteronomy 30:14.

Jesus is the closest parallel. He ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders, one who hears and acts and one who hears and does not, Matthew 7:24 to 27, and in Luke asks why people call Him Lord and do not do what He says, Luke 6:46. In the parable of the sower the seed is the word, and fruit is the proof it was received, Mark 4:14 to 20. Paul says the same thing with different vocabulary: it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous, Romans 2:13, and faith expresses itself through love, Galatians 5:6.

The implanted word echoes the promises of the new covenant, that God would put His law in the mind and write it on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and give a new heart and His Spirit so that His people would walk in His statutes, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. Peter uses the same seed language for new birth through the living and enduring word of God, 1 Peter 1:23. The care of orphans and widows has its roots in God's own character, Psalm 68:5, and passes into the life of the early church, Acts 6:1 to 6 and 1 Timothy 5:3 to 16.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James wrote as a pastor who had watched a particular kind of failure, people who knew the right things and enjoyed hearing them, and whose lives had not moved. He is not trying to unsettle those who are genuinely trying to obey; the man who looks intently and continues is called blessed. His target is comfort. The danger he exposes is the quiet belief that agreeing with the word is the same as being changed by it, and he wants his readers to feel the foolishness of walking away from a mirror and forgetting a face.

He also wants them to see where obedience is hardest to fake. Anger and speech are the two places where a person is most easily exposed, so he begins and ends the passage there. A reader who accepts the word and yet snaps at his family, fills his talk with careless words and overlooks the widow down the road has not yet looked into the mirror at all.

Finally James wants his hearers to be encouraged. The word is planted, it is able to save, and the law it contains is a law of freedom. He is not asking for a burden to be lifted onto weak shoulders; he is describing what the saving word does when it is welcomed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost every verb in this section is a command: be quick to listen, get rid of filth, accept the word, be doers. The mirror and the pure religion of verse 27 are illustrations meant to be applied directly. The care is in what the commands do not say. They do not tell us to earn salvation by obeying, since the word is already described as planted and able to save. They do not make hearing worthless either, since receiving the word comes first and is itself a command.

Verse 27 is also not a full definition of everything religion involves. James does not deny worship, prayer or doctrine elsewhere in his letter. He picks two outward marks that are easily neglected and names them as the evidence that the rest is real. Today that means the passage should drive believers toward concrete mercy and a disciplined mouth, without being used to dismiss gathered worship or sound teaching.

debates.question: What is the 'word planted in you which can save your souls'?

views.label: The gospel message received at conversion
views.case: James has just said that God gave us birth by the word of truth, verse 18, and Peter likewise ties new birth to the living and enduring word, 1 Peter 1:23. On this reading the planted word is the gospel that was sown at conversion, and the command to accept it describes humble, ongoing welcome of what has already taken root.

views.label: The whole word of God, gospel and commands together
views.case: Others point out that the word is also something a person is told to do, verse 22, and that it is spoken of as law in verse 25. So it is the entire revelation of God, the saving message and its demands as one, received into the heart as the new covenant promised, Jeremiah 31:33.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the word is God's gift rather than human achievement, and that its saving power is shown in a changed life. Neither allows hearing alone to be treated as the end.

debates.question: Does 'save your souls' mean final salvation or something short of it?

views.label: Final salvation, from judgment
views.case: James uses the language of salvation elsewhere for rescue from judgment, James 2:14 and 4:12, and the whole letter looks toward the coming of the Lord, James 5:7 to 9. On this view the word is the instrument by which a person is finally saved, and the commands tell what the saved life is like.

views.label: Deliverance in the present life
views.case: Others suggest the verse describes the preserving, healing work of the word in believers, the way it rescues the whole person from the destructive pull of anger and filth that the verse tells them to put off.

debates.bearing: The final reading fits the letter's horizon most naturally, and the present benefits are real consequences of it. James is warning that an unobeyed word leaves the hearer deceived about where he stands.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 19 begins with a short, balanced triple: quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. The adjectives are tachys and bradys, and the Greek sets the ear against the mouth and the temper with the same two adjectives, so the verse is built like a proverb. James is not asking for silence; he is asking for an order of operations, with listening first.

In verse 21 James uses a clothing metaphor. 'Get rid of' is a participle from the verb apotithemi, to lay aside, the same verb used of taking off clothes, and Paul uses the idea of putting off the old self and putting on the new in Ephesians 4:22 to 24. The thing laid aside is rhyparia, filth, and perisseia kakias, which is literally the surplus or overflow of evil. The word rhyparos, from the same root, describes the poor man's dirty clothes in 2:2, so the filth James tells us to put off is the very thing the poor man is accused of wearing, a quiet irony.

The planted word is the emphytos logos. The adjective means grown in, rooted, which gives a picture of a seed already sown in the soil rather than a message tossed at the listener. The command that goes with it is dexasthe, an aorist imperative of dechomai, to receive or welcome, which is the verb used of welcoming a guest. The word is to be welcomed, not merely tolerated.

Verse 22 warns against being deceived. The verb is paralogizomai, to reason falsely, which pictures a mind that has talked itself into something wrong. The self deception is not ignorance but flawed logic: I heard it, so I have done it. The doer is the poietes, from the verb poieo, to do or make, and the word appears in the phrase poietes ergou, a doer of work, in verse 25. In verse 23 the man looks at 'his face' in Greek 'the face of his birth', a phrase that suggests the face he was born with, his natural face, so the mirror shows him who he really is.

Verse 25 is the centre. The verb behind 'looks intently' is parakypto, which literally means to stoop or bend over to look, as Peter and Mary do at the empty tomb, John 20:5 and 20:11. The person looking into the law does not glance from a distance; he bends over it. He is said to continue, from parameno, to remain beside, so that his doing is persistent. The law he studies is called 'perfect', teleios, the word James uses elsewhere for the mature and complete, 1:4, and 'of liberty', the law that gives freedom.

Verse 26 introduces the verb chalinagogeo, to bridle, which James uses only here and in 3:2. The image of the horse's bit returns in 3:3 and links this passage with the next. The noun threskeia, religion, in verses 26 and 27, refers to the outward practice of worship, rites and observance. James turns it on its head by saying its truest form is not liturgical but moral. Finally ephiskeptomai in verse 27, to visit or look after, is the word used of God's care of His people, Luke 1:68, so caring for orphans and widows is described in the vocabulary of divine visitation.

typology.type: The planted word, a seed in the soil
typology.fulfillment: Scripture often pictures God's word as seed that bears fruit in the heart, from Isaiah 55:10 to 11, where rain and snow water the earth so that it yields seed for the sower, to the parable of the sower, Mark 4:14 to 20. James's emphytos logos belongs in that family. The correspondence reaches its fullness in new birth by the living word, 1 Peter 1:23, and in the Word who became flesh, John 1:14. The picture falls short of the whole truth if it suggests that the word acts mechanically. James still commands the hearer to receive and do.

typology.type: The mirror and the unveiled face
typology.fulfillment: James's mirror shows a person his own face, and what it reveals is meant to be acted on. Paul uses the same image for believers who, with unveiled faces, behold the glory of the Lord and are transformed into His image, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The escalation in Christ is that the mirror is no longer only a standard that exposes us but a glory that remakes us. The type falls short because James is describing the exposing work of the law, which is a different, earlier moment than the transforming sight Paul describes, though both belong together.

typology.type: The law of liberty and the new covenant law
typology.fulfillment: Under the old covenant the law was written on stone and often felt like a weight, Acts 15:10. The prophets promised a day when God would write His law in minds and on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, and give His Spirit to move people to obey, Ezekiel 36:27. James's phrase, the perfect law of freedom, stands on that promise. In Christ the demand has not shrunk, but the power has come, and Paul can say believers have been set free from sin and become slaves to righteousness, Romans 6:18. The type falls short in that the old law could not itself give the heart to keep it.

typology.type: Care for the orphan and widow, God's own work
typology.fulfillment: The law and the Psalms describe God as the defender of widows and the father of the fatherless, Psalm 68:5, and Israel was told to imitate Him, Deuteronomy 10:18 to 19. In Jesus the visit of God becomes literal. He raises the widow of Nain's son and gives him back to her, Luke 7:11 to 15, and from the cross entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple, John 19:26 to 27. The church's care for widows in Acts 6 and 1 Timothy 5 carries it forward. The correspondence is incomplete in that no human care can reverse the deepest loss, which waits for the resurrection.

study.christ:
Christ is the first and perfect doer of the word. The Gospel of John calls Him the Word, John 1:1 and 1:14, and says He came not to do His own will but the will of Him who sent Him, John 6:38. Where James describes a man who forgets what he has seen, Jesus is the man who never forgets and always does. He could say, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me,' John 4:34. In that sense the 'perfect law of freedom' is not only a set of commands but a person who obeyed them without remainder.

Christ also supplies the freedom in the phrase. The law that exposes a hearer in the mirror cannot, by itself, make him a doer. Paul says that what the law was powerless to do, God did by sending His own Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, Romans 8:3 to 4. James's doer is therefore not a lone moralist trying harder. He is a person born by the word of truth, James 1:18, in whom the word has been planted by the Spirit that Jesus promised, John 14:26.

The pattern of mercy in verse 27 leads straight to Him. Jesus is the one who visits the helpless, the God who has looked on His people, Luke 1:68, and in the parable of the sheep and goats He makes care for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner the test of everyone who claims to know Him, Matthew 25:35 to 40. He also stands behind the other test, the bridled tongue. When reviled, He did not revile in return, 1 Peter 2:23, and His words are called the words of eternal life, John 6:68. His mouth is the model of speech that is slow to anger and quick to bless.

Finally, Christ is the one who answers the failure the mirror exposes. If the mirror shows us as forgetful hearers, who have not done what we know, then the gospel is that He bore the judgment owed to such people and gives them a new heart. The warning of James is not meant to leave us with only a sharper conscience; it is meant to send us back to the One who is the true Doer and who makes doers of those who trust Him, Ephesians 2:10. We should avoid forcing every detail of James into a picture of Christ, but the central thread, that the Word became flesh and did the word perfectly for us, is firmly there.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the giver of a word and a Father who wants it done. The language is relational from the start. The word is the word of truth by which He gave birth, 1:18, and the religion He accepts is offered 'before our God and Father,' verse 27. James does not picture a remote lawgiver demanding obedience from strangers. He pictures a Father whose children are expected to look like Him, and whose word is the means of their being His children in the first place.

God is also shown as a God who speaks in order to be understood and done. The word is planted, which is the way of someone who wants it to take root, and it is a law that gives freedom, which is the way of someone who wants His people free rather than crushed. The law and the freedom are not opposed in James. God's commands are the shape of a good life, and the person who keeps them is blessed in what he does, verse 25. That blessing is not an additional reward stacked on top; it is the way the life God intends actually works.

He is a God of purity and of mercy at once. The two marks of verse 27, care for the weak and separation from the world's pollution, correspond to two sides of His own character: He defends the helpless, Psalm 68:5, and He is holy, so that those who belong to Him are called to be holy as well, 1 Peter 1:15 to 16. James will not let mercy become softness toward sin or purity become coldness toward need.

Verse 20 adds a quiet but important note, that 'man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.' God is not served by our heat, however righteous it feels. The righteousness He wants is His own, produced by His word working in the humble, and not by the urgency of our reactions. For worship this means that listening is itself an act of reverence, that obedience is the natural fruit of hearing, and that the Father who gave birth by the word of truth will finish what He started in those who welcome it.

crossReferences.note: Jesus' closing parable of the two builders is the nearest parallel to James's hearer and doer. Both builders hear; only one acts, and the storm tests the house. James's mirror gives the same lesson in a quieter image: the harm of hearing without doing is not seen at once but at the moment of crisis.

Paul says that it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers who will be declared righteous. Set beside James 1:22 it shows that Paul and James both reject the idea that hearing is enough. Paul writes against pride in privilege, James against passive comfort, and both want obedience.

The promise to put God's law in the mind and write it on the heart is the background to the word 'planted' in James. It explains how a law can be called a law of freedom: under the new covenant the law is no longer only outside the believer but also within, and brings with it the desire to obey.

God promises a new heart and His own Spirit, causing His people to walk in His statutes. This is the other half of the picture. James commands the doing, and Ezekiel shows where the power to do it comes from. The pattern of command and promise sits together in both texts.

Peter says believers are born again through the living and enduring word of God. Together with James 1:18, this shows that the word is the means of new birth as well as the standard of the new life, which is why James can say the planted word is able to save.

In the parable of the sower the word is the seed, and the different soils show the different outcomes. Only the good soil bears a crop. The parable explains what James means by receiving the word: reception is measured by fruit, and some hearers hear gladly and fall away.

Paul also speaks of looking at a mirror, but there he looks at the glory of the Lord and is transformed into His image. It deepens James's picture. The word shows us ourselves, and the Lord who speaks through it, as we keep looking, makes us like Himself.

God executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. This is the ground of James 1:27. Care for the vulnerable is not an invention of the early church; it is what the character of God requires of those who belong to Him.

The psalmist prays, 'Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth.' It shows that the bridled tongue of James 1:26 is not simply a matter of effort. The same prayer admits the need for God's help, which prepares the way for the stronger statements about the tongue in chapter 3.

The King says that what was done for the hungry, the stranger and the imprisoned was done for Him. This makes the care for the needy in James 1:27 more than ethics: it is a measure of how people have treated Christ, and a visible sign of whether the word has taken root.

The short mention of the unbridled tongue in 1:26 is taken up at length in chapter 3, where the same verb for bridling appears in 3:2. Read together, the two passages show that the tongue is the place where hearing and doing are most easily tested.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with God speaking, and creation comes into being by His word, Genesis 1. Humanity falls when it stops listening to that word and believes another voice, Genesis 3:1 to 6. From then on the question that runs through the whole of Scripture is whether people will hear and do. Israel at Sinai promised to do all God said, Exodus 24:7, and repeatedly failed, so that the prophets complain of a people with ears that do not hear, Jeremiah 5:21. James 1:19 to 27 stands in that long conversation and answers it with a pastoral urgency: the word has been planted, so do it.

What it answers from before is the failure of the old covenant to produce a heart that obeys. Moses told Israel that the word was near them, Deuteronomy 30:14, yet the generation after generation left it unobeyed. The prophets promised a new covenant in which God would write His law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, and give His Spirit, Ezekiel 36:27. James writes as someone living on the far side of that promise. The word that is planted in believers, and the law that gives freedom, are the fruit of what God promised.

What the passage sets up is the rest of James and the letters that share its concern. The call to care for the helpless runs into the warnings against favoritism in chapter 2, the demonstration of living faith in chapter 2, and the call to patient endurance in chapter 5. The tongue, brought up in verse 26, gets its fuller treatment in chapter 3. The same insistence that faith expresses itself in love is found in Paul, Galatians 5:6, and John, 1 John 3:18.

The story ends where it began, with a people who hear God's voice and live by it. In the new creation the law is no longer written on stone or learned from another but known by all, Hebrews 8:10 to 11, and the people of God finally look like the One whose image they bear, Romans 8:29. The mirror of James is then no longer a place of exposure but of delight, and the persistent doing he commands becomes the natural life of those who see Him as He is, 1 John 3:2. Until then, every small act of listening, every curbed word and every visit to a widow is an early fruit of that new creation.

quiz.q: Why does James warn against being merely a hearer of the word?

options.text: Because hearing without doing deceives us, like glancing in a mirror and forgetting our face.
options.note: Verses 22 to 24: the danger is self-deception through unpracticed hearing.

options.text: Because the one who does the word will be blessed in what he does.
options.note: True from verse 25, stating the positive side of the same command.

options.text: Because hearing the word is unimportant.
options.note: James values hearing; he insists it must lead to doing, not that it is worthless.

options.text: Because only teachers are meant to obey the word.
options.note: The command to do the word is for every believer, not only teachers.

quiz.q: What does James say about human anger?

options.text: It does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
options.note: Verse 20: man's anger fails to produce God's righteousness.

options.text: We should be slow to it, quick to listen, and slow to speak.
options.note: True from verse 19, the command that flows from verse 20.

options.text: It is always sinful and can never be righteous.
options.note: James targets man's anger that works against righteousness, not every possible anger.

options.text: It is a reliable engine for godly living.
options.note: The text says the opposite: it does not produce God's righteousness.

quiz.q: How does James describe the perfect law of liberty?

options.text: Something to look into intently and keep doing, bringing blessing to the doer.
options.note: Verse 25: sustained gazing and doing, not a passing glance.

options.text: God's freeing word that we obey rather than merely hear.
options.note: True to the sense of the law of liberty, though it omits the promised blessing.

options.text: A heavy burden that condemns everyone who reads it.
options.note: James calls it the law of liberty precisely because it frees rather than crushes.

options.text: A set of rituals to perform on holy days.
options.note: The passage contrasts true religion with mere ritual.

quiz.q: What does James call pure and undefiled religion before God?

options.text: Caring for orphans and widows in distress and keeping oneself unstained by the world.
options.note: Verse 27: practical mercy joined to personal holiness.

options.text: Bridling the tongue so that one's religion is not worthless.
options.note: True from verse 26, another mark of genuine religion.

options.text: Attending worship faithfully and keeping the ceremonies.
options.note: James redefines religion beyond ceremony to mercy and holiness.

options.text: Speaking often and confidently about spiritual things.
options.note: He warns against an unbridled tongue, not toward more talk.

quiz.q: How should the saving word be received, according to verse 21?

options.text: Humbly, after getting rid of moral filth and evil.
options.note: Verse 21: put off wickedness and meekly accept the implanted word.

options.text: As a seed planted in us that has power to save our souls.
options.note: True to the image of the implanted word, though the stress is on how we receive it.

options.text: Only after we have first proven ourselves worthy.
options.note: It is received in humility, not earned by prior worthiness.

options.text: With indifference, since hearing changes nothing.
options.note: The word can save the soul, so it is to be received humbly and obeyed.

questions: James says to be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Which of the three do you find hardest, and where did it show this week?
Is there a part of God's word you have heard clearly but have not yet done? What would obedience actually look like there?
The forgetful hearer glances in the mirror and walks away unchanged. What helps you look intently into God's word and keep doing it, rather than forgetting?
James measures real religion by a bridled tongue, care for the vulnerable, and a life unstained by the world. Which of these is God pressing on you right now?
Who are the orphans, widows, or distressed people God has placed near you, and how could you care for one of them this week?

translationNotes.note: The word planted in you renders the implanted word, an image of a seed sown in the heart; it is the same saving word introduced in verse 18.
Religion here renders threskeia, outward religious worship and practice; James redefines it by its fruit rather than abolishing it.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for James 1:19-27.
